extracted.intended_audience: poets, painters, orators, artists, critics, and students of aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for producing and evaluating the sublime and the beautiful in poetry, painting, and rhetoric, focusing on passions (self-preservation, society, sympathy), terror, obscurity, power, and imitation. Guidance is aimed at creators and critics who wish to affect or judge the passions with precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation versus the nature of the object
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the object represented in poetry or painting is such as we could have no desire of seeing them in the reality, then I may be sure that its power in poetry or painting is owing to the power of imitation, and to no cause operating in the thing itself." (still-life examples)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the depicted object is one we would not seek in reality (e.g., a dunghill, kitchen utensils), its appeal comes from the skill of imitation. Conversely, if we would run to see the object in real life, the power is due to the nature of the thing itself rather than mere imitation. Use this distinction to judge whether a work's effect arises from representation or from the intrinsic quality of its subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition as a driver of improvement and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: "God has planted in man a sense of ambition, and a satisfaction arising from the contemplation of his excelling his fellows in something deemed valuable amongst them... it is this passion that drives men to all the ways we see in use of signalizing themselves..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition gives pleasure when a work or action suggests superiority or distinction. In artistic/critical contexts, scenes or passages that allow the reader to feel exalted or superior (or that evoke the subject's ambition) can produce pleasurable effects; flattery and the idea of preference exploit this. Consider how portrayals of distinction or triumph will arouse ambition-derived pleasure in audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime defined as delight from ideas of pain and danger (self-preservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The passions which belong to self-preservation, turn on pain and danger... they are simply painful when their causes immediately affect us; they are delightful when we have an idea of pain and danger, without being actually in such circumstances; whatever excites this delight, I call sublime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce the sublime, evoke ideas of pain, danger, or threat in a way that the audience contemplates them without actually undergoing them. Recognize that passions tied to self-preservation are among the strongest and form the basis for sublime effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal passions: love and the idea of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two sorts of societies... The passion belonging to [sex] is called love... The other is the great society with man and all other animals. The passion subservient to this is called likewise love... its object is beauty... which is a name I shall apply to all such qualities in things as induce in us a sense of affection and tenderness..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty and love are rooted in positive pleasure and induce affection/tenderness; they can be mixed with uneasiness (e.g., fear of losing the object). When aiming for beautiful effects, emphasize qualities that induce tenderness and positive pleasure; when mixing with loss or danger, expect more complex, mixed passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy as the mechanism for conveyed passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The particular passion under this head called sympathy has the greatest extent. The nature of this passion is, to put us in the place of another, in whatever circumstance he is in, and to affect us in a like manner..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use devices that enable audiences to 'stand in another's place' (vivid perspective, narrative empathy, dramatic depiction) to transmit passions effectively. Sympathy can turn on either pain or pleasure and is a central route for affecting an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study passions and observe nature as the true standard of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and artists have often sought rules in other works rather than nature; "The true-standard of the arts is in every man's power; and an easy observation of the most common... things in nature, will give the truest lights..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging art, prefer observation of nature and human passions over imitation of existing artworks or following critics' rules. Critical knowledge of the boundaries and operations of passions is necessary to affect them 'after a delicate manner' and to judge works properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astonishment as the highest effect of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The passion caused by the great and sublime in nature... is astonishment; and astonishment is that state of the soul, in which all its motions are suspended, with some degree of horror... Astonishment... is the effect of the sublime in its highest degree; the inferior effects are admiration, reverence, and respect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce astonishment — a suspension of ordinary cognitive motion combined with awe/horror — for the strongest sublime effect. Lesser effects include admiration and reverence; structure the work to escalate toward astonishment when maximal sublimity is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror as a principal source of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "NO passion so effectually robs the mind of all its powers of acting and reasoning as fear... Whatever therefore is terrible, with regard to sight, is sublime too... terror is in all cases... the ruling principle of the sublime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate elements that inspire fear or apprehension (not merely size) to evoke sublimity. Small but dangerous creatures (serpents, poisons) and large things imbued with terror (the ocean) can both be sources of the sublime. Consider cultural/linguistic affinities between wonder and fear when crafting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity heightens terror and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "To make anything very terrible, obscurity seems in general to be necessary... night adds to our dread... popular tales... keep their idol in a dark part... Milton's description of Death... is admirably studied; it is astonishing with what a gloomy pomp, with what a significant and expressive uncertainty... he has finished the portrait of the king of terrors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ obscurity, vagueness, and darkness (literal or figurative) to amplify terror; specific, clear depiction often reduces dread. Use uncertainty and suggestiveness to provoke the imagination and make the fearful appear greater than any clear representation could.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness versus obscurity regarding affect on the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is one thing to make an idea clear, and another to make it affecting to the imagination... a great clearness helps but little towards affecting the passions, as it is in some sort an enemy to all enthusiasms whatsoever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor evocative, sometimes obscure verbal description over precise, clear imagery when the goal is to move passions; poetry (with its obscurity) can have a broader and more powerful dominion over passions than painting. Balance clarity where needed with obscurity to sustain affective power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowding great/confused images to approach infinity and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The mind is hurried out of itself, by a crowd of great and confused images; which affect because they are crowded and confused. For, separate them, and you lose much of the greatness: and join them, and you infallibly lose the clearness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evoke a sense of infinity and sublime magnitude, assemble multiple vast, interrelated images in a crowded, somewhat confused manner. This increases emotional impact but sacrifices clearness; use this technique deliberately when grandeur rather than clarity is the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power (physical strength/force) as a modification of the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "Besides those things which directly suggest the idea of danger... I know of nothing sublime, which is not some modification of power... the affection arising from the idea of vast power... is extremely remote from that neutral character... strength, violence, pain, and terror, are ideas that rush in upon the mind together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray power as potentially harmful or uncontrollable to create sublimity. Emphasize the capacity for force, violence, or domination rather than usefulness. If strength is shown as harmless or subservient (useful animals, domesticated power), it tends toward contempt rather than the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and social power evoke awe and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The power which arises from institution in kings and commanders, has the same connexion with terror... Sovereigns are frequently addressed with the title of dread majesty... young persons... are commonly struck with an awe which takes away the free use of their faculties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representations of authority, sovereignty, or commanding social power to produce awe and sublime effects. Consider audience experience: inexperience or unfamiliarity with power increases awe. Addressing or depicting high authority in terms of 'dread' amplifies sublimity.
